# Common fractions and the rule of three (`fractions_rule_of_three`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/math.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Mathematics & measurement (`math`)
- Deps: helped by arabic_numerals
- Core idea: A fraction is a number written as numerator over denominator; to add fractions bring them to a common denominator, to multiply them multiply tops and bottoms, to divide by a non-zero fraction multiply by its reciprocal, and reduce by the greatest common divisor (found by repeated subtraction for positive integers, Euclid's algorithm). The rule of three solves every proportion problem of trade: if a things cost b, then c things cost b x c / a (multiply first, divide last). With it one converts currencies, weights and measures, shares profits and mixes alloys.
- Pitfalls:
  - Adding numerators and denominators separately (1/2 + 1/3 is 5/6, not 2/5).
  - Applying direct proportion to an inverse relation (more workers need less time, not more).
  - Assuming every culture wrote general fractions. Egyptians used almost only unit fractions, Romans twelfths, Babylonians sexagesimal places.
  - Dividing before multiplying in the rule of three and losing accuracy through rounding.
- History: mesopotamia: c. 2000–1800 BC – sexagesimal fractions and tables of reciprocals; division is multiplication by the reciprocal; egypt: c. 1550 BC – Rhind papyrus (copy of a text c. 1850 BC), sums of unit fractions and a table for 2/n; greece: c. 370 BC – Eudoxus' theory of proportion (Euclid, Elements V); c. 300 BC Euclid's algorithm (Elements VII); rome: duodecimal fractions of the as (uncia = 1/12), used for money, weights and inheritances; china: c. 1st c. AD – Nine Chapters, ch. 1 full arithmetic of common fractions with reduction by mutual subtraction, ch. 2 rule of three (jin you); india: 499 – Aryabhata states the rule of three (trairashika); fractions written numerator above denominator without a bar (Bakhshali manuscript, Brahmagupta 628); islamic: 12th c. – al-Hassar (Maghreb) writes the horizontal fraction bar; europe: 1202 – Fibonacci uses the fraction bar; 14th–16th c. the rule of three is the 'golden rule' of the abbaco schools and printed arithmetics
- Read:
  - Gay Robins & Charles Shute, The Rhind Mathematical Papyrus: An Ancient Egyptian Text (1987)
  - Frank J. Swetz, Capitalism and Arithmetic: The New Math of the 15th Century (1987)
  - Shen Kangshen, John N. Crossley & Anthony W.-C. Lun, The Nine Chapters on the Mathematical Art: Companion and Commentary (1999)
